title: Adjectives III (Word formation)
description: Use prefixes, suffixes and sentence clues to form the right adjective.
objectives: Use meaning and grammar to choose the form

source.title: Advanced Grammar & Vocabulary — Express Publishing
source.note: Lesson vocabulary, examples and written tasks follow the supplied pages. Definitions are condensed for readability; spacing and obvious scan errors are corrected. Hints, explanations and model answers are study aids, not a publisher answer key.

lessons.title: Adjectives, related nouns and opposites
lessons.body: The document gives adjectives, meanings, related noun forms and opposites. Study the complete word family alongside the original example: accessible/accessibility/inaccessible, accurate/accuracy/inaccurate, and coherent/coherence/incoherent.

lessons.title: Negative forms and word families
lessons.body: Learn each negative prefix with its word. The exercise supplies un-, dis-, ir-, il-, ab-, im- and in-. The original examples below also show several opposites in use.

lessons.title: Form the adjective that fits
lessons.body: Exercise 2 supplies these suffixes: -ish, -ial, -ed, -able, -ive, -less, -ible and -ic. Check whether the sentence requires a positive or negative meaning. Preferential treatment, practical ideas and responsible behaviour are among the document’s combinations.

vocabulary.definition: Easy to reach, enter or use.
vocabulary.example: The northern part of the park is virtually inaccessible unless you have a four-wheel drive.
It is not always easy to give accurate measurements for the strength of an earthquake.
Audrey was extremely apologetic for having kept us waiting so long.

vocabulary.definition: Open to debate, or possible to argue.
vocabulary.example: Whether or not this is the way forward is arguable. / It is arguable that education leads to higher income.
I've never met anyone more argumentative than Jenny; she will tell you that black is white.
This is a clear and coherent explanation of the workings of the internal combustion engine.

vocabulary.definition: Able to make firm decisions promptly.
vocabulary.example: Winston Churchill's decisive policies rallied the country round him at a difficult and dangerous time.

vocabulary.definition: Careful not to embarrass others or reveal private information.
vocabulary.example: Try to be as discreet as possible as he's very sensitive and easily upset.
Don't you think that a 25% price increase is excessive, even allowing for inflation?
Malcolm is knowledgeable about computer hardware and will tell you everything you want to know.
I can't possibly read this; her handwriting is illegible.
There is no logical explanation for his behaviour.
A loyal friend will stand by you through good and bad times.
It's not abnormal for boys of his age to want to join the army.

vocabulary.definition: Doing what you are told to do.
vocabulary.example: Jo is a very disobedient child and refuses to do what she is told.
This is the only official biography of the author currently on the market.
He always gets outstanding results, despite his unorthodox teaching methods.

vocabulary.definition: Believable or reasonably likely to be true.
vocabulary.example: The special effects in the film were excellent but I didn't think the plot was very plausible.
Timothy was a polite young man with impeccable manners.

vocabulary.definition: Sensible and likely to work in real situations.
vocabulary.example: Banning all vehicles from the city centre is a lovely idea but I don't think it's practical at all.
This machine has brought an unprecedented degree of precision to the business of dating trees.

vocabulary.definition: Giving someone an advantage over others.
vocabulary.example: Harry gets preferential treatment at work, with an office all to himself, just because he is the boss's nephew.
Many of the paintings lost in the fire were irreplaceable old masters.
vocabulary.note: opposite: irreplaceable; not identical to disposable.

vocabulary.example: Sharon is the perfect employee; hardworking and responsible.

vocabulary.definition: Fully developed and ready to eat.
vocabulary.example: I'm not buying these tomatoes; they're unripe.

vocabulary.definition: Very careful to act honestly and fairly.
vocabulary.example: Socrates was known for his scrupulous adherence to the truth and his refusal to compromise.

exerciseGroups.title: Exercise 2 · Form an adjective
exerciseGroups.instruction: Use the capitalised word to form an adjective. You may need a prefix or a suffix.

questions.prompt: I may be related to the Managing Director, but believe me, I don't get ___ treatment. (PREFER)
questions.explanation: Suggested form: preferential. Read it in the whole sentence to check the meaning.
questions.hint: The answer starts with “p”.

questions.prompt: You are 25 years old and you are acting like a spoilt schoolboy. Stop being so ___. (CHILD)
questions.explanation: Suggested form: childish. Read it in the whole sentence to check the meaning.
questions.hint: The answer starts with “c”.

questions.prompt: Ben hated it, but I thought it was a very interesting and ___ programme. (INFORMATION)
questions.explanation: Suggested form: informative. Read it in the whole sentence to check the meaning.
questions.hint: The answer starts with “i”.

questions.prompt: This is the worst ___ crisis that this country has had to face in over 100 years. (ECONOMY)
questions.explanation: Suggested form: economic. Read it in the whole sentence to check the meaning.
questions.hint: The answer starts with “e”.

questions.prompt: Why are you being so ___? You're disagreeing with everything I say. (ARGUE)
questions.explanation: Suggested form: argumentative. Read it in the whole sentence to check the meaning.
questions.hint: The answer starts with “a”.

questions.prompt: Appearances can be ___. He might look aggressive but really he is as gentle as a lamb. (DECEIVE)
questions.explanation: Suggested form: deceptive. Read it in the whole sentence to check the meaning.
questions.hint: The answer starts with “d”.

questions.prompt: ___ with the money he was receiving, Sid decided to leave the company. (SATISFY)
questions.explanation: Suggested form: dissatisfied. Read it in the whole sentence to check the meaning.
questions.hint: The answer starts with “d”.

questions.prompt: For some ___ reason, she gave up her job, sold everything she owned and went to live on a desert island. (EXPLAIN)
questions.explanation: Suggested form: inexplicable. Read it in the whole sentence to check the meaning.
questions.hint: The answer starts with “i”.

questions.prompt: All the judges gave her ten out of ten. She had given a ___ performance. (FLAW)
questions.explanation: Suggested form: flawless. Read it in the whole sentence to check the meaning.
questions.hint: The answer starts with “f”.

questions.prompt: He looked terrible. Too much work and too many ___ nights. He had to get away. (SLEEP)
questions.explanation: Suggested form: sleepless. Read it in the whole sentence to check the meaning.
questions.hint: The answer starts with “s”.

questions.prompt: He can be very ___ when he wants to. He can talk you into anything. (PERSUADE)
questions.explanation: Suggested form: persuasive. Read it in the whole sentence to check the meaning.
questions.hint: The answer starts with “p”.

questions.prompt: The best man was very embarrassed and very ___ about forgetting the time that the wedding was to take place. (APOLOGISE)
questions.explanation: Suggested form: apologetic. Read it in the whole sentence to check the meaning.
questions.hint: The answer starts with “a”.

exerciseGroups.passage: What kind of 0) educational experience and background should we be giving our children? In a 1) ___ western economy, they need to be well-informed and 2) ___. In a complex ever-changing modern world, it is 3) ___ that the task of preparing the next generation cannot be carried out within the 4) ___ classroom framework, because acquiring a proper education in this way is simply 5) ___. This is where computer-aided learning steps in, providing children with the skills that they will need in tomorrow's world, in a one-to-one learner-centred environment. There are those who claim, however, that 6) ___ exposure to computers may prove to be harmful rather than 7) ___ to children and that it is more 8) ___ for education to take place in the classroom. They say that, although computers seem to hold a(n) 9) ___ appeal for some people, particularly young children, it is 10) ___ for children to have a person, rather than a machine, for a teacher.
